answer.answer: Yes, subject to terms. Ransomware and Cyber Extortion (II.I) pays cyber extortion expenses, which include money or virtual currency paid at the direction and demand of the extortionist, but only with Coalition's prior written consent. It is on this quote with a $1,000,000 limit and a $2,500 retention, and the payment erodes the aggregate limit. The cost of responding to the extortion is also covered, and forensics through Coalition Incident Response carry no retention.

answer.answer: Yes. Insuring Agreement J covers business interruption loss and extra expenses when computer systems are interrupted longer than the waiting period by a security failure (such as a ransomware attack) or a systems failure. On this quote J has a $1,000,000 limit, a $2,500 retention and an 8-hour waiting period (1 hour for a denial of service attack where a panel DDoS vendor is used). Coverage is limited to the indemnity period, which is capped at 180 days, and the client must submit a signed proof of loss within 90 days of discovery.

citations.quote: partial or complete interruption of computer systems for a period longer than the waiting period caused by a security failure or systems failure

However, in no event will the indemnity period exceed 180 days.
you must complete and sign a written, detailed, and affirmed proof of loss within 90 days after your discovery of the security failure

answer.answer: Yes, this looks like the Funds Transfer Fraud and Social Engineering coverage (II.Q), which is on the quote with a $250,000 limit and a $2,500 retention. A spoofed email impersonating a vendor that directs a wire fits the definition of funds transfer fraud, so the $40,000 loss would fall within the sublimit, less the retention. The fraud must have been first discovered during the policy period and reported through the Item 8 contacts, and the claim is subject to the policy's exclusions.

answer.answer: Yes. Breach Response Costs (II.G) covers the costs to notify affected individuals and to provide up to two years of credit or identity monitoring (longer if required by law). The costs must be reasonable and necessary, incurred with our prior written consent, and incurred within one year of discovering the breach. This quote shows a $1,000,000 limit and a $2,500 retention for this coverage.

answer.answer: Yes. Under Network and Information Security Liability, the policy pays claim expenses and damages when someone makes a claim against the practice for a security failure, data breach, or privacy liability. The insurer has the right and duty to defend a claim seeking damages payable under the policy, and the practice can choose defense counsel from the panel. Defense costs reduce the limit, are subject to the $2,500 retention, and the claim must be first made and reported during the policy period. Exclusions such as Prior Knowledge or the Retroactive Date could still limit coverage.

any claim against you seeking damages that are payable under the terms of this Policy
The Limits of Liability of this Policy will be reduced and may be completely exhausted by payment of claim expenses.

answer.answer: No. The policy excludes losses arising from a physical event or natural disaster, and flood is named specifically, so a flood destroying the server room would not be covered. Coverage here is built around security failures and systems failures, and the systems failure definition also excludes loss of or damage to physical equipment or property. The tangible property exclusion would also apply to damaged hardware, apart from the narrow computer replacement and bricking coverage, which is tied to a security failure.

citations.quote: Any physical event or natural disaster, including but not limited to fire, flood, earthquake
loss of or damage to any physical equipment or property
Any injury or damage to, destruction, impairment, or loss of use of any tangible property

answer.answer: Generally no. The policy excludes electrical or mechanical failure or outage of a utility or other third party, including electricity providers, so a power company outage that shuts the practice for a day is not covered. The only exception is business interruption coverage where the loss comes directly from a service provider experiencing its own security failure, which a plain power outage is not. Also, business interruption only pays for interruption longer than the waiting period (8 hours on this quote), and only when caused by a security failure or systems failure.

citations.quote: Electrical, mechanical failure, or interruption (including blackouts, brownouts, power surge, or outage) of a utility or other third party
where such loss arises directly from a service provider directly experiencing their own security failure
caused by a security failure or systems failure first discovered by you during the policy period

answer.answer: Yes, potentially. Insuring Agreement M (Computer Replacement and Bricking) pays reasonable and necessary costs to restore or replace hardware impacted by a loss of firmware integrity resulting from a security failure, and it is on this quote with a $1,000,000 limit and $2,500 retention. The tangible property exclusion carves M out, so hardware is not excluded here. Costs need our prior written consent, and the hardware must be owned or leased by the practice. Note that laptops owned by employees and not used for business operations are not a security failure.

to restore or replace computer hardware or tangible equipment owned or leased by you impacted by a loss of firmware integrity resulting from a security failure
except this exclusion will not apply to coverage afforded under Section II.M, COMPUTER REPLACEMENT AND BRICKING
